newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua sees higher grain output as growth boon.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua sees higher grain output as growth boon.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman on Thursday unveiled his government's agriculture strategy for 1997-98, promising to make impoverished Nicaragua "Central America's granery" through market-oriented reforms.
Aleman's agriculture minister, Mario de Franco, said Nicaragua's agricultural production was projected to rise by 18 percent in 1997, led by rising grain production.

Aleman, a right-wing lawyer and coffee farmer who took office on Jan. 10, said reviving Nicaragua's moribund agricultural sector would be his government's top economic priority and the spark for its economic growth in 1997, projected by the government to be 6.8 percent.

Nicaragua, with the largest land mass in Central America, was a major food exporter before years of civil war in the late 1970s and 1980s disrupted output and turned Nicaragua into a net food importer.

To reverse this trend, the plan, called the "Policy and Action Framework for the 1997-98 Agricultural Cycle," proposed the elimination of various taxes on farmers, greater reliance on private banks for financing and the privatization of the state grains marketing system.

Central Bank President Noel Ramirez said that under the plan, private banks will double the money they give to the agricultural sector this cycle to about $109 million, while state banks would chip in $33 million.

"The measures appear good to me. For me the problem is whether the benefits of the reforms really reach the producer. I see some gaps," Eduardo Rizo, executive president of the Nicaraguan Union of Coffee Growers, told Reuters.
Farmers feared the government's move to have private banks finance farmers will lead to the bankruptcy of small and medium-sized farmers, who are less attractive borrowers, Rizo said.
Juan Tijerino, President of the Nicaraguan National Cattle Commission, said Nicaragua's private banks lack the necessary capacity to finance farmers and asked for more financing by state banks.
